subject: Effificent implementation of fitting different priors to the same data set

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: Effificent implementation of fitting different priors to the same data set
parts:
Dear all,

Let's say I want to fit a simple linear model with user supplied prior

data {
  int N;       // some very large value
  vector[N] y;
  vector[N] x;

  real prior_b;
  real prior_b_sd;
}

parameters {
  real b;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

model {
  y ~ normal (b * x, sigma);
 
  b ~ normal (prior_b, prior_b_sd);
}


Question: Now instead of a single set of prior spec, i want to be able to able to compute a set of b's given different priors. The use case can to understand how different (informative) priors can affect b given the same data set.

The data block can look like this:
data{
...
  int<lower=1> N_p
  real prior_b[N_p];
  real prior_b_sd[N_p];
}

But, what's the best way to code up the model block?

A naive approach can be:
parameters {
  real b[N_p];
  real<lower=0> sigma[N_p];
}

model {
  for (i in 1:N_p) {
    y ~ normal (x * b[i], sigma[i]);
  }

  // priors
  b ~ normal (prior_b, prior_b_l);
  a ~ normal (prior_a, prior_a_l);
}

But, this would involve "sampling" N_p times for exactly the same data set (y, x) for the same intermediate results as the difference comes from the different priors.

Is there any way I can compute the log_prob of b using the data set (y, x) once and then apply the prior spec over this value to form each b[i]?

Many thanks,

Andy

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effificent implementation of fitting different priors to the same data set
parts:
I don't think there's a much more efficient way to do it than what
you're proposing in a single model. It might be faster to run
separate programs for each value of the prior.

We've never really pursued the lasso-style path estimation where you
fit with a vague prior, then use the fitted values to initialize a fit
with slightly less vague prior and so on (or maybe it's the other way
around --- I can never remember which way they compute). I doubt
it'll help much if you have to generate an n_eff > 10.

- Bob

P.S. We tend to follow Andrew's convention of writing:

alpha ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);

To sort out which priors go with which variables.
It sort of breaks down at the second level of hierarchy, where we'd
get mu_mu_alpha and what not.

Of course, your naming convention's up to you!
